create.title: 1. You create a transaction
create.text: Your wallet picks a few boxes to spend, signs with your secret key and sends it to a node.

mempool.title: 2. Into the mempool
mempool.text: The node checks the transaction is valid, then relays it to other nodes. It waits in a “waiting room” called the mempool.

mine.title: 3. Miners pack it into a block
mine.text: Miners pick transactions from the mempool, assemble a block and race to solve the Proof-of-Work puzzle.

update.title: 4. Every node updates
update.text: The winning block is broadcast. Every node re-checks all of it independently, then appends it to its own chain.

intro: Ergo is a network of many computers around the world, all keeping a copy of the same ledger. There is no central server. So how do they agree on who owns how much? This article answers that question.

node.title: Nodes: the record keepers
node.p1: A node is a computer running the Ergo software. It downloads the entire blockchain history, checks every block and every transaction against the rules, and talks to other nodes (called peers).
node.p2: The key point: every node checks everything for itself. If someone sends a fraudulent block — say, one that prints extra ERG — every honest node rejects it. Nobody needs to be “trusted”.
node.live: The node serving data for this page is {{name}}, currently connected to {{peers}} peers.

journey.title: The journey of a transaction
journey.mempool: Right now there are {{n}} transactions waiting in the node's mempool to be included in the next block.
journey.figAlt: The journey of a transaction: 1. your wallet signs it, 2. it waits in a node's mempool, 3. a miner packs it into a block while guessing numbers, 4. every node checks the new block and adds it to its chain.
journey.figCaption: A transaction goes from your wallet, through the mempool and a miner's block, to every node's copy of the chain.

blocks.title: Blocks and the chain
blocks.p1: Transactions aren't recorded one by one; they're grouped into blocks. On Ergo a new block appears roughly every 2 minutes on average. Every block has a fingerprint: a short code (called a hash) that changes completely if even one character in the block changes. That fingerprint is the block's id, and each block also stores the id of the block before it — its parent id. That's how blocks link together into a chain:
blocks.p2: If someone wanted to change an old transaction, the id of the block containing it would change, which makes the next block's parent id wrong, and the one after that… The attacker would have to re-mine every block from that point up to today, faster than the rest of the network combined. In practice, that's all but impossible.

miners.title: Miners and Proof-of-Work
miners.p1: Who gets to write the next block? The answer is a Proof-of-Work contest — a lottery you win by guessing fast. Miners keep changing one spare number inside their block (the nonce) and recomputing a special hash of the block (the proof-of-work puzzle), billions of times, until that hash comes out small enough to count as a win (below a limit called the target). The first miner to get there broadcasts the block and collects a reward in newly created ERG.
miners.p2: Finding a solution takes a lot of work, but checking one is extremely fast. That's why a laptop running a node can verify the effort of the entire mining network. See <mining>Mining Ergo</mining> for details.

confirm.title: Confirmations
confirm.p1: When your transaction lands in a block, it has 1 confirmation. Every new block mined on top adds one more. The more confirmations, the harder the transaction is to reverse. For everyday payments a few confirmations (a few minutes) is plenty; for large amounts, exchanges usually wait longer.

try.title: Try it
try.text: Open the <explorer>latest block</explorer> in the explorer, then come back a few minutes later — you'll see its confirmation count go up.

next.title: What's next
next.p1: You now know where a transaction goes. But what's inside one? On Ergo, the answer is boxes — read <boxes>Boxes: where the money lives</boxes>.
